arguments.title: Returns change, April 2011 vs May 2011 (calendar month), by country
arguments.interpretation: Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both requested calendar months are fully in range. Policy retail-gbp-v1 defines returns as the absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations, in GBP; it is not cash collected, and bookkeeping/return adjustments remain in source. Per the saved comparison, total returns rose from the April baseline to the May current period (delta positive). Per the saved country breakdown (top 8 plus OTHER, 23 groups in OTHER, reconciled to totals), the United Kingdom was the largest positive contributor, while Singapore and Japan fell to zero in the current period and France and Australia declined; Portugal and Channel Islands appear only in the current period. These are descriptive additive contributions only; the breakdown tool reports causal=false. No causal claim is made. Note that country-level swings to or from zero may reflect where return lines were recorded rather than a change in underlying customer behavior.
hypotheses: The United Kingdom increase may reflect a genuine rise in returned volume or value, or a shift in where return lines were booked; the data cannot distinguish these.
Singapore and Japan dropping to zero returns in May could indicate no returns occurred, or that returns were recorded under a different country/entity in that month.
Portugal and Channel Islands appearing only in May may reflect new return activity or reclassification of existing activity.
Month-to-month return swings may be driven by a small number of large cancellation invoices rather than broad-based change; this would require line-level inspection to test.

args.interpretation: Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both requested calendar months are fully in range. Policy retail-gbp-v1 defines returns as the absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations, in GBP; it is not cash collected, and bookkeeping/return adjustments remain in source. Per the saved comparison, total returns rose from the April baseline to the May current period (delta positive). Per the saved country breakdown (top 8 plus OTHER, 23 groups in OTHER, reconciled to totals), the United Kingdom was the largest positive contributor, while Singapore and Japan fell to zero in the current period and France and Australia declined; Portugal and Channel Islands appear only in the current period. These are descriptive additive contributions only; the breakdown tool reports causal=false. No causal claim is made. Note that country-level swings to or from zero may reflect where return lines were recorded rather than a change in underlying customer behavior.
hypotheses: The United Kingdom increase may reflect a genuine rise in returned volume or value, or a shift in where return lines were booked; the data cannot distinguish these.
Singapore and Japan dropping to zero returns in May could indicate no returns occurred, or that returns were recorded under a different country/entity in that month.
Portugal and Channel Islands appearing only in May may reflect new return activity or reclassification of existing activity.
Month-to-month return swings may be driven by a small number of large cancellation invoices rather than broad-based change; this would require line-level inspection to test.

WITH periods AS (SELECT 'baseline' period, ?::TIMESTAMP a, ?::TIMESTAMP b UNION ALL SELECT 'current', ?::TIMESTAMP, ?::TIMESTAMP)
      SELECT p.period, coalesce(sum(CASE WHEN quantity < 0 THEN -(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price) ELSE 0 END),0)::VARCHAR value, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN quantity > 0 AND NOT starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') THEN invoice_no END)::VARCHAR orders
      FROM periods p LEFT JOIN facts f ON invoice_time >= p.a AND invoice_time < p.b AND (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) GROUP BY p.period ORDER BY p.period

details.interpretation: Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both requested calendar months are fully in range. Policy retail-gbp-v1 defines returns as the absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations, in GBP; it is not cash collected, and bookkeeping/return adjustments remain in source. Per the saved comparison, total returns rose from the April baseline to the May current period (delta positive). Per the saved country breakdown (top 8 plus OTHER, 23 groups in OTHER, reconciled to totals), the United Kingdom was the largest positive contributor, while Singapore and Japan fell to zero in the current period and France and Australia declined; Portugal and Channel Islands appear only in the current period. These are descriptive additive contributions only; the breakdown tool reports causal=false. No causal claim is made. Note that country-level swings to or from zero may reflect where return lines were recorded rather than a change in underlying customer behavior.
hypotheses: The United Kingdom increase may reflect a genuine rise in returned volume or value, or a shift in where return lines were booked; the data cannot distinguish these.
Singapore and Japan dropping to zero returns in May could indicate no returns occurred, or that returns were recorded under a different country/entity in that month.
Portugal and Channel Islands appearing only in May may reflect new return activity or reclassification of existing activity.
Month-to-month return swings may be driven by a small number of large cancellation invoices rather than broad-based change; this would require line-level inspection to test.

arguments.title: Returns, May 2011 vs April 2011 (calendar month), with country breakdown
arguments.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both requested calendar months are fully inside coverage; no partial-period caveat applies. Policy retail-gbp-v1 defines returns as the absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations, in GBP; it is a bookkeeping measure, not cash refunded. Per the catalog, duplicate source lines are preserved and return adjustments remain in source, so figures are descriptive only.

Comparison (ev_cbd6a81c...): returns rose from the April 2011 baseline to the May 2011 current period, a positive delta. All quantitative values are in the evidence record.

Country breakdown, top 8 plus OTHER (ev_ee979276...): the increase is not broad-based. The United Kingdom is the single largest positive contributor and by itself exceeds the total net change, meaning other countries net out negative. Singapore and Japan show returns in the baseline and none in the current month, and France, Australia and Switzerland also declined; these are the main offsets. Portugal and Channel Islands show no baseline returns and new current-period returns. The OTHER bucket (23 remaining countries) is small and slightly negative. Top-8 plus OTHER reconciles exactly to the comparison totals, so no unexplained residual exists.

Interpretation limits: the breakdown is additive and descriptive. The concentration in the United Kingdom and the appearance/disappearance of returns in specific countries are consistent with a small number of large return or cancellation events rather than a shift in underlying return propensity, but this dataset view cannot distinguish those. No causal claim is made.
hypotheses: A small number of large-value return or cancellation lines in the United Kingdom drove most of the month-over-month increase, rather than a broad rise in return frequency.
The Singapore and Japan baseline returns with zero current-month returns reflect one-off cancellation events in April rather than a durable improvement in those markets.
The new Portugal and Channel Islands current-month returns reflect isolated large adjustments rather than newly established return activity.
Because returns include cancellation invoices, part of the movement may reflect invoice-timing/bookkeeping effects (when cancellations were recorded) rather than changes in customer return behavior.

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both requested calendar months are fully inside coverage; no partial-period caveat applies. Policy retail-gbp-v1 defines returns as the absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations, in GBP; it is a bookkeeping measure, not cash refunded. Per the catalog, duplicate source lines are preserved and return adjustments remain in source, so figures are descriptive only.

Comparison (ev_cbd6a81c...): returns rose from the April 2011 baseline to the May 2011 current period, a positive delta. All quantitative values are in the evidence record.

Country breakdown, top 8 plus OTHER (ev_ee979276...): the increase is not broad-based. The United Kingdom is the single largest positive contributor and by itself exceeds the total net change, meaning other countries net out negative. Singapore and Japan show returns in the baseline and none in the current month, and France, Australia and Switzerland also declined; these are the main offsets. Portugal and Channel Islands show no baseline returns and new current-period returns. The OTHER bucket (23 remaining countries) is small and slightly negative. Top-8 plus OTHER reconciles exactly to the comparison totals, so no unexplained residual exists.

Interpretation limits: the breakdown is additive and descriptive. The concentration in the United Kingdom and the appearance/disappearance of returns in specific countries are consistent with a small number of large return or cancellation events rather than a shift in underlying return propensity, but this dataset view cannot distinguish those. No causal claim is made.
hypotheses: A small number of large-value return or cancellation lines in the United Kingdom drove most of the month-over-month increase, rather than a broad rise in return frequency.
The Singapore and Japan baseline returns with zero current-month returns reflect one-off cancellation events in April rather than a durable improvement in those markets.
The new Portugal and Channel Islands current-month returns reflect isolated large adjustments rather than newly established return activity.
Because returns include cancellation invoices, part of the movement may reflect invoice-timing/bookkeeping effects (when cancellations were recorded) rather than changes in customer return behavior.

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 to 2011-12-09, so both requested calendar months are fully inside coverage; no partial-period caveat applies. Policy retail-gbp-v1 defines returns as the absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations, in GBP; it is a bookkeeping measure, not cash refunded. Per the catalog, duplicate source lines are preserved and return adjustments remain in source, so figures are descriptive only.

Comparison (ev_cbd6a81c...): returns rose from the April 2011 baseline to the May 2011 current period, a positive delta. All quantitative values are in the evidence record.

Country breakdown, top 8 plus OTHER (ev_ee979276...): the increase is not broad-based. The United Kingdom is the single largest positive contributor and by itself exceeds the total net change, meaning other countries net out negative. Singapore and Japan show returns in the baseline and none in the current month, and France, Australia and Switzerland also declined; these are the main offsets. Portugal and Channel Islands show no baseline returns and new current-period returns. The OTHER bucket (23 remaining countries) is small and slightly negative. Top-8 plus OTHER reconciles exactly to the comparison totals, so no unexplained residual exists.

Interpretation limits: the breakdown is additive and descriptive. The concentration in the United Kingdom and the appearance/disappearance of returns in specific countries are consistent with a small number of large return or cancellation events rather than a shift in underlying return propensity, but this dataset view cannot distinguish those. No causal claim is made.
hypotheses: A small number of large-value return or cancellation lines in the United Kingdom drove most of the month-over-month increase, rather than a broad rise in return frequency.
The Singapore and Japan baseline returns with zero current-month returns reflect one-off cancellation events in April rather than a durable improvement in those markets.
The new Portugal and Channel Islands current-month returns reflect isolated large adjustments rather than newly established return activity.
Because returns include cancellation invoices, part of the movement may reflect invoice-timing/bookkeeping effects (when cancellations were recorded) rather than changes in customer return behavior.

Treat explanations as unverified; keep hypotheses separate.

arguments.title: Net sales, 2011-02-15→2011-03-01 vs 2011-02-01→2011-02-15 (equal 14-day periods), with stock_code breakdown
arguments.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (source local wall time, no timezone inferred), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on invoice-line grain, restricted to unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, and preserving duplicate source lines; it is explicitly not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f301cf89ee1cfdde957fe846dfbc9c06d3ccae11fc34a28d7088e5f5c1 for exact figures).

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd825d9ef320affd404d9410f6e4af7941edda7d6f093c2b1da0e5102b): the change is not concentrated in the top 12 codes. The OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the largest single positive contribution and is larger than the net total change, meaning the top-12 codes collectively offset part of the OTHER increase. Within the top 12, the largest negative contributions come from AMAZONFEE (a fee/adjustment code, not a merchandise item, moving from zero to a negative amount) and several numeric product codes that fell sharply; the largest positive contributions come from a different set of numeric product codes. Breakdown totals reconcile exactly to the comparison totals, and the tool marks the breakdown as descriptive, not causal.

Interpretation limits: net_sales includes bookkeeping and return adjustments, so part of the movement reflects fee/return postings rather than underlying demand. The AMAZONFEE line in particular is an adjustment-type code, so its contribution should not be read as a product-level sales decline. No causal claim is made.
hypotheses: The AMAZONFEE negative contribution may reflect a fee or adjustment posting recorded in the current window rather than a change in merchandise demand; this is a bookkeeping artifact hypothesis, not established.
The broad-based positive movement in the OTHER bucket (2,405 codes) may indicate a general uplift in order volume or basket size across many small-volume products rather than a few large items.

Sharp declines in specific numeric product codes (e.g. 21623, 22693, 22189) may reflect stock availability, end-of-life, or one-off bulk purchases in the baseline window; requires order-level or inventory data to test.

Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and 135,080 rows lack customer IDs, some of the change may come from unattributed transactions; customer-level attribution would be needed to test this.

details.title: Net sales, 2011-02-15→2011-03-01 vs 2011-02-01→2011-02-15 (equal 14-day periods), with stock_code breakdown

evidence.sql:
WITH periods AS (SELECT 'baseline' period, ?::TIMESTAMP a, ?::TIMESTAMP b UNION ALL SELECT 'current', ?::TIMESTAMP, ?::TIMESTAMP)
      SELECT p.period, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN quantity > 0 AND NOT starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') THEN invoice_no END)::VARCHAR orders
      FROM periods p LEFT JOIN facts f ON invoice_time >= p.a AND invoice_time < p.b AND (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) GROUP BY p.period ORDER BY p.period

catalog.time: Source local wall time; no timezone inferred
catalog.grain: invoice line; orders use distinct invoice_no; customers use nonempty customer_id
catalog.eligibility: unit_price > 0; exclude cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity; preserve duplicate source lines
catalog.net_sales: Signed eligible quantity × unit_price; not cash collected
catalog.gross_sales: Eligible positive-quantity sales, excluding cancellation invoices
catalog.returns: Absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations
catalog.sales_orders: Distinct invoices with eligible positive sales
catalog.identified_customers: Distinct known customers with eligible positive sales; unknown customers still contribute revenue
catalog.avg_order_value: Gross sales / distinct sales orders; four-decimal half-away-from-zero rounding
catalog.caveat: Bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in source; contribution is descriptive, not causal

evidence.sql:
SELECT stock_code dimension, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, CASE WHEN invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP THEN 'baseline' ELSE 'current' END period
      FROM facts WHERE (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) AND ((invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP) OR (invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP)) GROUP BY dimension, period ORDER BY dimension, period

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (source local wall time, no timezone inferred), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on invoice-line grain, restricted to unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, and preserving duplicate source lines; it is explicitly not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f301cf89ee1cfdde957fe846dfbc9c06d3ccae11fc34a28d7088e5f5c1 for exact figures).

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd825d9ef320affd404d9410f6e4af7941edda7d6f093c2b1da0e5102b): the change is not concentrated in the top 12 codes. The OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the largest single positive contribution and is larger than the net total change, meaning the top-12 codes collectively offset part of the OTHER increase. Within the top 12, the largest negative contributions come from AMAZONFEE (a fee/adjustment code, not a merchandise item, moving from zero to a negative amount) and several numeric product codes that fell sharply; the largest positive contributions come from a different set of numeric product codes. Breakdown totals reconcile exactly to the comparison totals, and the tool marks the breakdown as descriptive, not causal.

Interpretation limits: net_sales includes bookkeeping and return adjustments, so part of the movement reflects fee/return postings rather than underlying demand. The AMAZONFEE line in particular is an adjustment-type code, so its contribution should not be read as a product-level sales decline. No causal claim is made.
hypotheses: The AMAZONFEE negative contribution may reflect a fee or adjustment posting recorded in the current window rather than a change in merchandise demand; this is a bookkeeping artifact hypothesis, not established.
The broad-based positive movement in the OTHER bucket (2,405 codes) may indicate a general uplift in order volume or basket size across many small-volume products rather than a few large items.

Sharp declines in specific numeric product codes (e.g. 21623, 22693, 22189) may reflect stock availability, end-of-life, or one-off bulk purchases in the baseline window; requires order-level or inventory data to test.

Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and 135,080 rows lack customer IDs, some of the change may come from unattributed transactions; customer-level attribution would be needed to test this.

evidence.sql:
WITH periods AS (SELECT 'baseline' period, ?::TIMESTAMP a, ?::TIMESTAMP b UNION ALL SELECT 'current', ?::TIMESTAMP, ?::TIMESTAMP)
      SELECT p.period, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN quantity > 0 AND NOT starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') THEN invoice_no END)::VARCHAR orders
      FROM periods p LEFT JOIN facts f ON invoice_time >= p.a AND invoice_time < p.b AND (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) GROUP BY p.period ORDER BY p.period

      FROM facts WHERE (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) AND ((invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP) OR (invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP)) GROUP BY dimension, period ORDER BY dimension, period

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (source local wall time, no timezone inferred), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on invoice-line grain, restricted to unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, and preserving duplicate source lines; it is explicitly not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f301cf89ee1cfdde957fe846dfbc9c06d3ccae11fc34a28d7088e5f5c1 for exact figures).

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd825d9ef320affd404d9410f6e4af7941edda7d6f093c2b1da0e5102b): the change is not concentrated in the top 12 codes. The OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the largest single positive contribution and is larger than the net total change, meaning the top-12 codes collectively offset part of the OTHER increase. Within the top 12, the largest negative contributions come from AMAZONFEE (a fee/adjustment code, not a merchandise item, moving from zero to a negative amount) and several numeric product codes that fell sharply; the largest positive contributions come from a different set of numeric product codes. Breakdown totals reconcile exactly to the comparison totals, and the tool marks the breakdown as descriptive, not causal.

Interpretation limits: net_sales includes bookkeeping and return adjustments, so part of the movement reflects fee/return postings rather than underlying demand. The AMAZONFEE line in particular is an adjustment-type code, so its contribution should not be read as a product-level sales decline. No causal claim is made.
hypotheses: The AMAZONFEE negative contribution may reflect a fee or adjustment posting recorded in the current window rather than a change in merchandise demand; this is a bookkeeping artifact hypothesis, not established.
The broad-based positive movement in the OTHER bucket (2,405 codes) may indicate a general uplift in order volume or basket size across many small-volume products rather than a few large items.

Sharp declines in specific numeric product codes (e.g. 21623, 22693, 22189) may reflect stock availability, end-of-life, or one-off bulk purchases in the baseline window; requires order-level or inventory data to test.

Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and 135,080 rows lack customer IDs, some of the change may come from unattributed transactions; customer-level attribution would be needed to test this.

Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (541,909 invoice lines), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage; no extrapolation was needed. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on lines with unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, preserving duplicate source lines; it is not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f3). This is a descriptive period-over-period change only.

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd): the change is not concentrated in the top movers — the OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the majority of the positive delta, while the largest single named movements are mixed in sign. The single largest named negative contributor is the code AMAZONFEE, which moves from zero in the baseline to a negative value in the current window; because net_sales is signed quantity × price, a negative contribution from a fee-type code reflects bookkeeping/return adjustments retained in the source rather than a product sales decline. Other notable named negatives are codes 21623, 22693, 22189 and 21137; notable named positives are 22053, 22423, 22197, 20749, 22084, 21621 and 21731. Named top-12 deltas and the OTHER delta reconcile exactly to the reported total delta, so the breakdown is additive and complete.

Interpretation limits: the catalog caveat states bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is descriptive, not causal. No causal claim is made here; the drivers below are untested hypotheses.
hypotheses: The negative AMAZONFEE contribution in the current window may reflect a fee/adjustment posting or reversal booked in that period rather than a change in product demand; this would need invoice-level inspection to confirm.
The large positive OTHER delta spread across ~2,405 stock codes may indicate broad-based basket growth or a shift in product mix rather than a few hero SKUs.
Named-code swings (e.g., 21623, 22693, 22189 down; 22053, 22423, 22197 up) may reflect stock availability, replenishment timing or one-off bulk orders rather than sustained demand change.
Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and negative quantities are retained, part of the movement may be attributable to returns/cancellation timing rather than new sales.
The current window extends into late February, so calendar effects (month-end ordering patterns) could contribute to the difference; this is untested.

details.title: Net sales, 2011-02-15→2011-03-01 vs 2011-02-01→2011-02-15 (equal 14-day periods), with stock_code breakdown

evidence.sql:
WITH periods AS (SELECT 'baseline' period, ?::TIMESTAMP a, ?::TIMESTAMP b UNION ALL SELECT 'current', ?::TIMESTAMP, ?::TIMESTAMP)
      SELECT p.period, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN quantity > 0 AND NOT starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') THEN invoice_no END)::VARCHAR orders
      FROM periods p LEFT JOIN facts f ON invoice_time >= p.a AND invoice_time < p.b AND (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) GROUP BY p.period ORDER BY p.period

catalog.time: Source local wall time; no timezone inferred
catalog.grain: invoice line; orders use distinct invoice_no; customers use nonempty customer_id
catalog.eligibility: unit_price > 0; exclude cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity; preserve duplicate source lines
catalog.net_sales: Signed eligible quantity × unit_price; not cash collected
catalog.gross_sales: Eligible positive-quantity sales, excluding cancellation invoices
catalog.returns: Absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations
catalog.sales_orders: Distinct invoices with eligible positive sales
catalog.identified_customers: Distinct known customers with eligible positive sales; unknown customers still contribute revenue
catalog.avg_order_value: Gross sales / distinct sales orders; four-decimal half-away-from-zero rounding
catalog.caveat: Bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in source; contribution is descriptive, not causal

      FROM facts WHERE (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) AND ((invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP) OR (invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP)) GROUP BY dimension, period ORDER BY dimension, period

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (541,909 invoice lines), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage; no extrapolation was needed. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on lines with unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, preserving duplicate source lines; it is not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f3). This is a descriptive period-over-period change only.

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd): the change is not concentrated in the top movers — the OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the majority of the positive delta, while the largest single named movements are mixed in sign. The single largest named negative contributor is the code AMAZONFEE, which moves from zero in the baseline to a negative value in the current window; because net_sales is signed quantity × price, a negative contribution from a fee-type code reflects bookkeeping/return adjustments retained in the source rather than a product sales decline. Other notable named negatives are codes 21623, 22693, 22189 and 21137; notable named positives are 22053, 22423, 22197, 20749, 22084, 21621 and 21731. Named top-12 deltas and the OTHER delta reconcile exactly to the reported total delta, so the breakdown is additive and complete.

Interpretation limits: the catalog caveat states bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is descriptive, not causal. No causal claim is made here; the drivers below are untested hypotheses.
hypotheses: The negative AMAZONFEE contribution in the current window may reflect a fee/adjustment posting or reversal booked in that period rather than a change in product demand; this would need invoice-level inspection to confirm.
The large positive OTHER delta spread across ~2,405 stock codes may indicate broad-based basket growth or a shift in product mix rather than a few hero SKUs.
Named-code swings (e.g., 21623, 22693, 22189 down; 22053, 22423, 22197 up) may reflect stock availability, replenishment timing or one-off bulk orders rather than sustained demand change.
Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and negative quantities are retained, part of the movement may be attributable to returns/cancellation timing rather than new sales.
The current window extends into late February, so calendar effects (month-end ordering patterns) could contribute to the difference; this is untested.

report.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (541,909 invoice lines), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage; no extrapolation was needed. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on lines with unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, preserving duplicate source lines; it is not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f3). This is a descriptive period-over-period change only.

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd): the change is not concentrated in the top movers — the OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the majority of the positive delta, while the largest single named movements are mixed in sign. The single largest named negative contributor is the code AMAZONFEE, which moves from zero in the baseline to a negative value in the current window; because net_sales is signed quantity × price, a negative contribution from a fee-type code reflects bookkeeping/return adjustments retained in the source rather than a product sales decline. Other notable named negatives are codes 21623, 22693, 22189 and 21137; notable named positives are 22053, 22423, 22197, 20749, 22084, 21621 and 21731. Named top-12 deltas and the OTHER delta reconcile exactly to the reported total delta, so the breakdown is additive and complete.

Interpretation limits: the catalog caveat states bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is descriptive, not causal. No causal claim is made here; the drivers below are untested hypotheses.
hypotheses: The negative AMAZONFEE contribution in the current window may reflect a fee/adjustment posting or reversal booked in that period rather than a change in product demand; this would need invoice-level inspection to confirm.
The large positive OTHER delta spread across ~2,405 stock codes may indicate broad-based basket growth or a shift in product mix rather than a few hero SKUs.
Named-code swings (e.g., 21623, 22693, 22189 down; 22053, 22423, 22197 up) may reflect stock availability, replenishment timing or one-off bulk orders rather than sustained demand change.
Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and negative quantities are retained, part of the movement may be attributable to returns/cancellation timing rather than new sales.
The current window extends into late February, so calendar effects (month-end ordering patterns) could contribute to the difference; this is untested.

details.title: Net sales, 2011-02-15→2011-03-01 vs 2011-02-01→2011-02-15 (equal 14-day periods), with stock_code breakdown

evidence.sql:
WITH periods AS (SELECT 'baseline' period, ?::TIMESTAMP a, ?::TIMESTAMP b UNION ALL SELECT 'current', ?::TIMESTAMP, ?::TIMESTAMP)
      SELECT p.period, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN quantity > 0 AND NOT starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') THEN invoice_no END)::VARCHAR orders
      FROM periods p LEFT JOIN facts f ON invoice_time >= p.a AND invoice_time < p.b AND (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) GROUP BY p.period ORDER BY p.period

catalog.time: Source local wall time; no timezone inferred
catalog.grain: invoice line; orders use distinct invoice_no; customers use nonempty customer_id
catalog.eligibility: unit_price > 0; exclude cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity; preserve duplicate source lines
catalog.net_sales: Signed eligible quantity × unit_price; not cash collected
catalog.gross_sales: Eligible positive-quantity sales, excluding cancellation invoices
catalog.returns: Absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations
catalog.sales_orders: Distinct invoices with eligible positive sales
catalog.identified_customers: Distinct known customers with eligible positive sales; unknown customers still contribute revenue
catalog.avg_order_value: Gross sales / distinct sales orders; four-decimal half-away-from-zero rounding
catalog.caveat: Bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in source; contribution is descriptive, not causal

evidence.sql:
SELECT stock_code dimension, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, CASE WHEN invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP THEN 'baseline' ELSE 'current' END period
      FROM facts WHERE (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) AND ((invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP) OR (invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP)) GROUP BY dimension, period ORDER BY dimension, period

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (541,909 invoice lines), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage; no extrapolation was needed. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on lines with unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, preserving duplicate source lines; it is not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f3). This is a descriptive period-over-period change only.

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd): the change is not concentrated in the top movers — the OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the majority of the positive delta, while the largest single named movements are mixed in sign. The single largest named negative contributor is the code AMAZONFEE, which moves from zero in the baseline to a negative value in the current window; because net_sales is signed quantity × price, a negative contribution from a fee-type code reflects bookkeeping/return adjustments retained in the source rather than a product sales decline. Other notable named negatives are codes 21623, 22693, 22189 and 21137; notable named positives are 22053, 22423, 22197, 20749, 22084, 21621 and 21731. Named top-12 deltas and the OTHER delta reconcile exactly to the reported total delta, so the breakdown is additive and complete.

Interpretation limits: the catalog caveat states bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is descriptive, not causal. No causal claim is made here; the drivers below are untested hypotheses.
hypotheses: The negative AMAZONFEE contribution in the current window may reflect a fee/adjustment posting or reversal booked in that period rather than a change in product demand; this would need invoice-level inspection to confirm.
The large positive OTHER delta spread across ~2,405 stock codes may indicate broad-based basket growth or a shift in product mix rather than a few hero SKUs.
Named-code swings (e.g., 21623, 22693, 22189 down; 22053, 22423, 22197 up) may reflect stock availability, replenishment timing or one-off bulk orders rather than sustained demand change.
Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and negative quantities are retained, part of the movement may be attributable to returns/cancellation timing rather than new sales.
The current window extends into late February, so calendar effects (month-end ordering patterns) could contribute to the difference; this is untested.

details.title: Net sales, 2011-02-15→2011-03-01 vs 2011-02-01→2011-02-15 (equal 14-day periods), with stock_code breakdown

evidence.sql:
WITH periods AS (SELECT 'baseline' period, ?::TIMESTAMP a, ?::TIMESTAMP b UNION ALL SELECT 'current', ?::TIMESTAMP, ?::TIMESTAMP)
      SELECT p.period, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN quantity > 0 AND NOT starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') THEN invoice_no END)::VARCHAR orders
      FROM periods p LEFT JOIN facts f ON invoice_time >= p.a AND invoice_time < p.b AND (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) GROUP BY p.period ORDER BY p.period

catalog.time: Source local wall time; no timezone inferred
catalog.grain: invoice line; orders use distinct invoice_no; customers use nonempty customer_id
catalog.eligibility: unit_price > 0; exclude cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity; preserve duplicate source lines
catalog.net_sales: Signed eligible quantity × unit_price; not cash collected
catalog.gross_sales: Eligible positive-quantity sales, excluding cancellation invoices
catalog.returns: Absolute amount of eligible negative-quantity lines, including cancellations
catalog.sales_orders: Distinct invoices with eligible positive sales
catalog.identified_customers: Distinct known customers with eligible positive sales; unknown customers still contribute revenue
catalog.avg_order_value: Gross sales / distinct sales orders; four-decimal half-away-from-zero rounding
catalog.caveat: Bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in source; contribution is descriptive, not causal

evidence.sql:
SELECT stock_code dimension, coalesce(sum(quantity::DECIMAL(18,0) * unit_price),0)::VARCHAR value, CASE WHEN invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP THEN 'baseline' ELSE 'current' END period
      FROM facts WHERE (unit_price > 0 AND NOT (starts_with(upper(invoice_no),'C') AND quantity >= 0)) AND ((invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP) OR (invoice_time >= ?::TIMESTAMP AND invoice_time < ?::TIMESTAMP)) GROUP BY dimension, period ORDER BY dimension, period

details.interpretation:
Dataset ds_1f8144bb8670bcad07cde082 covers 2010-12-01 08:26 to 2011-12-09 12:50 (541,909 invoice lines), so both requested 14-day windows are fully inside coverage; no extrapolation was needed. Policy retail-gbp-v1, currency GBP: net_sales is signed eligible quantity × unit_price on lines with unit_price > 0, excluding cancellation invoices with nonnegative quantity, preserving duplicate source lines; it is not cash collected. Quality flags noted: 135,080 unknown customers, 1,454 missing descriptions, 2,517 nonpositive prices, 10,624 negative quantities, 0 inconsistent cancellations, 0 invalid required fields.

Comparison (equal_days, 14 days each): net_sales rose from the baseline window to the current window, with a positive delta (see evidence ev_b720f3f3). This is a descriptive period-over-period change only.

Breakdown by stock_code (top 12 plus OTHER, ev_e70330bd): the change is not concentrated in the top movers — the OTHER bucket (2,405 groups) carries the majority of the positive delta, while the largest single named movements are mixed in sign. The single largest named negative contributor is the code AMAZONFEE, which moves from zero in the baseline to a negative value in the current window; because net_sales is signed quantity × price, a negative contribution from a fee-type code reflects bookkeeping/return adjustments retained in the source rather than a product sales decline. Other notable named negatives are codes 21623, 22693, 22189 and 21137; notable named positives are 22053, 22423, 22197, 20749, 22084, 21621 and 21731. Named top-12 deltas and the OTHER delta reconcile exactly to the reported total delta, so the breakdown is additive and complete.

Interpretation limits: the catalog caveat states bookkeeping and return adjustments remain in the source and that contribution is descriptive, not causal. No causal claim is made here; the drivers below are untested hypotheses.
hypotheses: The negative AMAZONFEE contribution in the current window may reflect a fee/adjustment posting or reversal booked in that period rather than a change in product demand; this would need invoice-level inspection to confirm.
The large positive OTHER delta spread across ~2,405 stock codes may indicate broad-based basket growth or a shift in product mix rather than a few hero SKUs.
Named-code swings (e.g., 21623, 22693, 22189 down; 22053, 22423, 22197 up) may reflect stock availability, replenishment timing or one-off bulk orders rather than sustained demand change.
Because unknown customers still contribute revenue and negative quantities are retained, part of the movement may be attributable to returns/cancellation timing rather than new sales.
The current window extends into late February, so calendar effects (month-end ordering patterns) could contribute to the difference; this is untested.
